First of all, to my dear colleague, Dmitry Ponomarev, who's the project manager at the EU-UN Global Terrorism Threats facility of UNOCT. As you have heard already, our two programs are working together with the Kyrgyz Republic, but not only. We also work in other countries around the world. Again, supporting the implementation of Security Council General Assembly mandates in the area of vulnerable targets protection. It's always a pleasure to work together, Dimitri, and I'll give you now the floor. Thank you.

Thank you very much, Ignacio. Excellencies, distinguished delegates, dear colleagues, allow me to add my welcome and thank you all for coming to this session today. And I would like to also acknowledge our excellent cooperation with the Kyrgyz Republic, CTAD, and OSCE in organizing this event and advancing this important area of work. Earlier, we heard from our colleagues from the Anti-Terrorism Center of the State Committee for National Security, who walked us through the journey of the Kyrgyz Republic in detail, from the initial assessment and identification of priorities and implementation of concrete actions, and strengthening of national capacities. This was structured national process that evolved over several years with support from the international community. What I would like to do in the next few minutes is to look at the same journey through a slightly different perspective. I will discuss the process from the perspective of United Nations Office of counterterrorism and illustrate how two UNOCT programmes supported the Kyrgyz Republic in— at different stages of this journey. The first is the Global Programme for the Protection of Vulnerable Targets, which supported national consultations, identification of priorities, the development of national-owned roadmap, and organization of study visit to Germany. Which exposed national counterparts to international good practices. Building on that foundation, the EU-UN Global Terrorism Threats Facility supported the implementation of those nationally identified priorities through expert mentoring, advisory support, targeted capacity building work, uh, support, uh, for development of technology-enabled solution, provision of equipment, and assistance in strengthening the legislative framework for critical infrastructure protection. UNOCT worked collaboratively with CTAD and coordinated our work closely with OECD program office in Bishkek. So, colleagues, what turns priorities in sustainable operation capacity? Many member states receive recommendations. Many develop strategies, but translating those priorities and strategies into sustainable operational capacity remains one of the greatest challenges that we have. In our experience, five elements are particularly important: national leadership and ownership; long-term partnership; targeted support responding to nationally identified priorities; And finally, focus on sustainable operational capacity rather than short-term outputs. The remainder of, remainder of my presentation will illustrate how these elements came together in the Kyrgyz Republic case study. Next slide, please. So building on the national priorities identified by the Kyrgyz Republic, UNOCT support through the Global Programme on Protection of Vulnerable Targets and the EU-UN Global Terrorism Threats Facility, focused on translating recommendations into nationally— national institutional capacity. This meant addressing several practical challenges. First, fragmented coordination. Through the leadership of the Anti-Terrorism Centre, This was addressed through establishment of interagency working group, bringing relevant national authorities into more structured coordination mechanism. Second, information management. Paper-based and fragmented information collection related to the protection of vulnerable targets is now being replaced by a secure online platform that supports the collection analysis, and sharing information among competent national authorities. Third, critical infrastructure protection framework. The Kyrgyz Republic is working to update its CIP framework, including through the development of modern legislation that reflects current risks, institutional responsibilities, and international good practices. Fourth, international experience. Through exchanges such as study visit to Germany, international experience was not simply copied. It was reviewed, adapted, and integrated into national capacity in a way that reflects legal, institutional, and operational specificities of the Kyrgyz Republic. And I would like to express our sincere appreciation to the Permanent Mission of Germany and the German national institutions that hosted the delegation and generously shared their experience with us. Through the UNOCT Global Programme on the Protection of Vulnerable Targets and the EU-UN Global Terrorist Threats Facility, the Kyrgyz Republic was able to access a range of international expertise and good practices. This included expert mentoring and advisory support, targeted capacity-building workshops, and international exchanges. But the important point is that this international experience was not treated as a model to be copied. It was reviewed, discussed, and adapted to the national context of the Kyrgyz Republic—its legal framework, institutional architecture, operational realities, and specific risk environment. In that sense, international expertise became a resource for developing national solutions. As our Kyrgyz colleagues described earlier, one of the most important elements of this process has been development of secure online platform. Through the EU-UN Global Terrorist Threat Facility, UNOCT supported these efforts by deploying expert— experts to assist with the development of the platform, but also providing IT equipment to help operate it effectively. The value of the online platform is very practical. It helps move from paper-based processes to structured information management. It will support analysis and should enable stronger coordination among national competent authorities. It can also help decision-makers access more reliable information when assessing risks prioritizing actions, or responding to incidents. At the same time, technology should not be seen as a quick solution to complex institutional challenges. A platform can support coordination, but it cannot lead coordination process. Equipment can enable action, but it cannot replace clear mandate procedures and institutional responsibilities. In our case study, technology was used to strengthen the ability of national authorities to collect information, analyze risks, coordinate actions, and make better informed decisions. But institutions remain at the center. Allow me to conclude with 5 broader lessons that we believe extend beyond the experience of one country. First, national leadership and ownership must always remain the foundation. Second, genuine partnership means that international actors support nationally defined priorities rather than directing them. Third, sustainable institutions development require long-term engagement. Capacity is built over years, not through isolated interventions. Fourth, the effective capacity building requires a diversity of tools that reinforce one another. In the case of the Kyrgyz Republic, this included deployment of experts for mentoring and advisory support, targeted capacity building workshops, international exchanges, access to good practices, legislative support, and as I mentioned before, provision of equipment. And these tools are most effective when they are not delivered as separate activities, but when they are sequenced and connected in support of one national-led process. It also important to know that throughout this process, uh, all activities were designed and delivered in accordance with the UN human rights standards, with human rights and gender considerations integrated across implementation, including through the application of human rights due diligence policy and appropriate risk mitigation measures. And finally, fifth, technology. It should be viewed as an enabler of institutional effectiveness, not as an objective in itself. Every member state's circumstances are different, but these principles are broadly applicable. They offer one practical model for translating counterterrorism priorities into sustainable national capacity. Although important progress has already been achieved, this process continues. Implementation must be followed by institutionalization. And institutionalization requires continuous learning and adaptation. Dear colleagues, as terrorism threats evolve, national systems must evolve as well. The experience of the Kyrgyz Republic demonstrates that sustainable progress is not a destination, but an ongoing process. Critical infrastructure protection is ultimately about resilience. And resilience depends on institutions that can anticipate risks, coordinate effectively, and continuously adapt to new threats. There is no single model for protecting critical infrastructure. Every country's institutions, legal frameworks, and threat environment are different, but targeted, tailored, coordinated, and sustainable international support can help member states to translate their own priorities into lasting institutional capacity and ultimately into strengthening national resilience. And I thank you.

Thank you, Mr. Moderator. Good morning, distinguished delegates, ladies and gentlemen. Let me begin by expressing my sincere appreciation to the government of the Kyrgyz Republic and the United Nations Office on Counterterrorism for co-organizing this timely and important discussion. For me, it is a pleasure to represent the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe, in this exchange today, and perhaps it is worth recalling at the outset that the OSCE is the largest regional security organization in the world with 57 participating states, and that its work is grounded in a comprehensive concept of security that brings together the political, military, economic, and environmental, and human dimensions. Today I would like to start my presentation with a simple question: What do the FIFA World Cup currently taking place here in the United States and the World Nomad Games that Kyrgyzstan will host this September have in common? At first glance, perhaps not much. Different geography, different scale, different audiences, yet from a security perspective they share remarkably similar challenges. Both events require large-scale crowd movements. Both require coordination among multiple agencies and stakeholders. Both require careful risk assessment, contingency planning and real-time decision-making under pressure. And both remind us of something that security professionals know well: success of a major event is often measured by what never happens. Behind every safe and successful event are months of planning, coordination, information sharing, and preparation that remain essential even if they are not immediately visible. And both highlight a very practical operational challenge: how to bring dozens of institutions together, each with different responsibilities, and transform them into a single coordinated effort. In many ways, this is exactly what our work in Kyrgyzstan has focused on over the past 2 years. From the OSCE perspective, the protection of vulnerable targets is ultimately about people. It is about ensuring that individuals can gather safely, participate in public life, attend cultural and sporting events, and enjoy public spaces without fear. Because vulnerable targets are not only infrastructure, they are the Spaces where societies come together, and protecting them requires much more than physical security measures. It requires planning, coordination, preparedness, and trust between institutions. Let me now turn to Kyrgyzstan— —where these principles have been translated into practical cooperation. Over the past 2 years, The OSCE program office in Bishkek, in close cooperation with colleagues from the OSCE Transnational Threats Department's project PROTECT, and its— in strong partnership with the Anti-Terrorism Center under the State Committee for National Security of the Kyrgyz Republic, has supported national efforts to strengthen approaches to the protection of vulnerable targets. This cooperation has been highly practical in nature. In 2025 and 2026, we supported a series of awareness-raising and capacity-building activities, bringing together key national stakeholders responsible for planning and securing public events. The focus was not theoretical, it was more operational. How do institutions plan together? How do they assess risk in a structured and proposed in a proportionate way? How do they coordinate responsibilities before an event takes place? And how do we ensure that security measures strengthen safety while respecting fundamental rights and freedoms? These were questions that guided our work. Um, one important outcome of this cooperation has been support for the development of a procedure for ensuring public order and security during the preparation and holding of mass events or public events in the Kyrgyz Republic, which was earlier mentioned by Aslanbek Abaev. This document is currently undergoing the final stages of national approval and is expected to be adopted in the coming weeks. What makes this development particularly important is that it establishes a unified framework for planning and coordinating security measures for public events in Kyrgyzstan. It introduces a structured and risk-based approach and clarifies institutional roles and responsibilities, and it supports more systematic classification of public events according to the scale and risk profile. In practical terms, it helps establish a shared operational language among different institutions responsible for public safety and security. As Kyrgyzstan prepares to host major, major events, including the upcoming World Nomad Games, such a framework can contribute to more effective planning, stronger coordination, and enhanced preparedness. Once this document is adopted, Our cooperation will move into the next phase focused on supporting its practical implementation. And this will include targeted capacity building activities to assist national stakeholders in applying the guidance in real operational setting and ensuring that the framework is effectively translated into day-to-day practice. Next slide, please. Our work in Kyrgyzstan has also benefited from the broader framework of the project PROTECT, an OSCE initiative led by the Action Against Terrorism, my colleague Daniel Goldstein, aimed at enhancing national approaches across the OSCE area to the protection of vulnerable targets from terrorist threats and other hazards. This project brings together three complementary elements. The development and dissemination of practical guidance and good practices, capacity building and training for national stakeholders, and the facilitation of regional cooperation and dialogue on effective protection measures. In this regard, I would like to acknowledge contributions of the United States and Germany, which have supported the implementation of Project Protect and its broader objectives across the OSCE region. Next slide, please. As part of this effort, the OSCE developed the Technical Guide on Physical Security of Critical Infrastructure, drawing on extensive consultations with practitioners, international experts, and partner organizations. The guide was developed with valuable contributions from the members of the expert expert advisory group, including UNOCT, IKEA, and Interpol. Importantly, the guide does not prescribe a single model. Rather, it seeks to bridge the gap between policy and practice by providing practical considerations that can support national authorities in strengthening the protection of vulnerable targets. Next slide, please. Here you can see the the technical guide in English and Russian. And on the right side, you can see that it was translated to several languages as well. The next slide. Alongside the technical guidance, we also recognized another challenge. Protecting critical infrastructure is not only a technical issue, it requires strategic understanding. Extending political attention and sustained senior-level commitment. To support this, the OSCE partnered with CEDIT, as mentioned earlier by Anna-Maria, uh, to update its early analytical work on the physical protection of critical infrastructure against terrorist attacks. The updated trends report was published in November 2025 in New York. The publication looks at the issue from a different angle. It takes stock of how the terrorist threat to critical infrastructure has evolved, highlights emerging risks such as the use of drones and AI, and outlines approaches that can strengthen national resilience at the strategic level. Together, the reports— the report complements the technical guide by connecting the why and what is changing with the how to respond, linking strategic threat understanding with practical action. Next slide, please. The experience of Kyrgyzstan also demonstrates a broader lesson. Progress in protecting vulnerable targets is most effective when national ownership is combined with practical international support. When national authorities define priorities and regional organizations contribute expertise and platforms for dialogue. And when international partners work together in a complementary manner. This is precisely the type of cooperation that today's side event seeks to highlight. And in the conclusion, I would like to reiterate that it— at its core, the protection of vulnerable targets is not about systems or procedures. It is about people. It is about whether our citizens feel safe together to participate and to experience public life without fear. And this is This is where the most important lesson from our work in Kyrgyzstan emerges. Progress in this field is never the result of the institution alone. It is the result of partnerships that connect national leadership with regional and international expertise. In Kyrgyzstan, this cooperation has brought together national authorities and regional partners, international experts, as well as— best practices from different jurisdictions. In Kyrgyzstan, it was experiences from the United Kingdom, France, Germany, and specialist institutions such as the International Center for Sports Security. And what matters is how different experiences can be translated into practical, locally owned solutions. And ultimately, this is what we are working towards— not only safer infrastructure, but safer public life, open, resilient, and shared. And I thank you.

We would like to first of all thank the Kyrgyz mission and the OCT and the OSCE for this event, which is a very timely event. These collaborations will highlight the importance of multilateral collaboration for joint cooperation. In an era where terrorism transcends national boundaries, the importance of standardized approaches and coordination cannot be emphasized enough. As a close regional partner of Kyrgyzstan, Pakistan values the engagement to face common threats in the terrorism domain that we face, particularly from Afghanistan, including which poses serious threats to international peace and security. Terrorist groups such as the TTP, BLA, and Majid Brigade, together with their affiliates of al-Qaeda and ISIL-K, have carried out a number of attacks in Pakistan— against vulnerable targets, and this includes public places, including schools, mosques, public transport, and infrastructure. Because no amount of protection can ensure a foolproof security guarantee for critical infrastructure and public places, namely the soft targets, if the supply side of logistics that enables terrorists to carry out attacks is not kept in check.— or blocked simultaneously. Therefore, this must be an integral part of our preventive efforts.

I thank you. I thank the delegation of Pakistan for your remarks. I now open the floor for any further comments or questions. Thank you very much. I don't see any further requests for the floor. UNOCT remains committed to supporting Member States in these efforts and to continuing this important work together with all of you.
